Who I am

When something serious comes up, I’m the one my friends call.

Whether they need advice, help with a car, or someone to show up and get something done, they know I’ll come through. That’s the kind of teammate I try to be everywhere: loyal, hard-working, and steady when things go sideways. When something goes wrong, I don’t panic. I slow down, figure out what actually needs to happen, and see it through.

I’m a car guy through and through, and I’m genuinely curious about how things work, why they fail, and how to make them better. That curiosity is how a shopping-cart go-kart turned into a six-year build, and why I’ll happily drive for hours on a Facebook Marketplace side quest if there’s a good project at the end of it. One of those side quests got me a broken lab furnace for free. I repaired it, and now I use it for material testing and annealing.

My dream car is a Bugatti Tourbillon. Someday I want to earn my pilot’s license, and my long-term goal is simple: a small house with a big shop.

Off the clock, I’m a well-rounded, laid-back guy. I played varsity football all four years of high school and loved it, and I still love watching a good game. Some of my favorite days are spent taking our jon boat out on the lake with my friends, bass fishing or chasing anything else that bites. I love going out to dinner, catching a concert, jamming out to good music, traveling, hiking, and being outdoors. I’m also a gamer: GTA V (and counting down to VI), Call of Duty, Rainbow Six Siege, and Fortnite back when everyone was playing it.

Whether you need a friend, a teammate, or someone on the shop floor, I’m someone you can count on.

Work

M4 Machine

CNC machining intern in Livingston, New Jersey, May to June 2026

In one month on the shop floor, I was trained by the shop’s lead engineer, owner, and floor operators to run CNC lathes, 4-axis mills, 5-axis mills, and a manual mill and lathe. I ran roughly 1,000 parts across 10 production programs in bronze, aluminum, steel, copper, and plastic.

I handled full setup for new jobs: proofing CAM programs, setting work offsets, changing tools, and squaring vises. I also built a workpiece swap routine that cut changeover downtime to as little as 15 seconds.

The catch I’m proudest of was a hairline crack forming in the base casting of one of the shop’s CNC lathes, the kind of defect that causes precision drift with no obvious explanation. I also traced recurring part defects back to their root causes instead of fixing each part as it came up. On the shop’s 5-axis CNC, I ran a precision fixture for a laser optics company; the machine consistently held 0.001 in. parallelism and 0.002 in. overall size, the tightest-tolerance job of my internship.

Livingston Ecolancers

Chief engineer and president of our Shell Eco-marathon team, 2023 to 2026

Ecolancers had gone dark during COVID, and as a sophomore I helped rebuild the team from the ground up. As chief engineer and president for my junior and senior years, I led a 20-student team and directed the powertrain, electrical, braking, and ergonomics work. It took three years of working through one engineering problem after another, but by senior year our car hit an officially verified 300 miles per gallon at Shell Eco-marathon Americas, held at the Indianapolis Motor Speedway. It passed Shell’s full technical and safety inspection both years I led the team.

Senior year, I replaced the magneto ignition with a Haltech ECU, wiring and programming it myself for full sequential fuel injection and electronically controlled ignition timing, with guidance I sourced from outside companies. I also designed two 3D-printed drivetrain parts: a gear-hub sprocket adapted to a standard mountain-bike sprocket, which saved the team $500 and a month of lead time over outsourcing, and a polycarbonate starter pulley with embedded one-way bearings. Both passed tech inspection and ran in competition.

The material choice came out of my own testing. I ran polycarbonate, PPA-CF, and PLA through heat-resistance and layer-strength tests in the lab furnace I repaired, which also showed us which parts were safe to print and which needed to stay metal. Along the way I worked out an efficient procedure for bleeding our single-master-cylinder, dual-caliper brakes, a problem the team hadn’t cleanly solved before, and I raised $2,000 in sponsor funding.

Go-kart design and fabrication

Independent project, 2020 to present

This build started in 7th grade as a modified shopping-cart frame. In 8th grade I welded my own frame, and since freshman year it’s been a purchased race chassis that I keep modifying. It has run four engines: a Predator 79cc, a Predator 212, a 250cc ATV engine, and now a 250cc dual-cylinder Kawasaki Ninja engine. Every step up meant balancing more power against weight, ground clearance, and safety. It reaches 60+ mph with ease and has a calculated top speed of 85 mph; the real limit so far has been finding enough room to test it.

The wiring harness was a project of its own. I first adapted the donor Ninja harness onto the kart and kept everything working, down to the horn and the dash gauges. Then I went back, fully unsleeved it, removed every redundant or dead circuit, and cut the bundle from a consistent 0.75 in. to under 0.5 in. before retaping it by hand, about six to eight focused hours of work.

I’ve also diagnosed and fixed two structural failures: a frame that bent under the added power, which I reheated, rewelded, and reinforced, and a snapped shifter linkage that I redesigned to be stronger. My MIG welding is self-taught, and my high school shop teacher taught me TIG. For precision parts beyond what my home shop can do, I work with local machine shops, and I’ve since modeled and 3D-printed smaller parts in Fusion 360.

Self-employed

Small engine repair and property services, 2020 to present

Since 7th grade I’ve run my own business doing small engine repair, handyman work, and seasonal snow and leaf removal. It adds up to 50 to 60+ jobs a season and roughly $20,000 in lifetime revenue, all from word of mouth and local Facebook groups with no paid advertising. On bigger jobs, I bring my friends on as hired help.

I source and repair my own used equipment wherever I can, and I maintain a full shop of hand tools, power tools, and outdoor equipment, from snowblowers to leaf blowers, that I use for both the business and my own builds.
